issues.description: The problem specification (UML) and the solution expect a StockIngredient constructor with three parameters (String name, int price, int quantity), but the template's StockIngredient class only provides a four-parameter constructor (String, int, int, boolean). This mismatch will confuse students and prevent them from instantiating StockIngredient using the signature shown in the exercise description and used in the solution.
issues.suggestedFix: Add a three-parameter constructor StockIngredient(String name, int price, int quantity) to the template's StockIngredient class (or overload the existing constructor) so it matches the UML in the problem statement and the solution. The new constructor can delegate to the existing implementation or perform the same validation logic, ensuring students can instantiate StockIngredient using the expected signature.

issues.description: The problem statement (and the example usage in Main.java) expect a StockIngredient constructor with signature StockIngredient(String, int, int), but the template's StockIngredient class only provides a constructor StockIngredient(String, int, int, boolean) (i.e., an extra 'strictValidation' parameter). The solution repository implements the 3-argument constructor. This mismatch in the constructor parameters (an identifier-level API difference) creates mapping confusion: students reading the problem and example will try to call a 3-arg constructor that does not exist in the template, forcing them to either modify the class or the examples and obscuring the intended API.
issues.suggestedFix: Provide a 3-argument constructor StockIngredient(String name, int price, int quantity) in the template (either by overloading the existing constructor or replacing it) so the API matches the problem statement and example Main usage. This aligns the template with the solution and the described class diagram, reducing student confusion.
